question: Trade receivables increased Rs 200cr during the year. In CFO this is:
before: Receivables increase = revenue recorded but cash not collected. Already in PAT (overstating cash), so subtract Rs 200cr. Equivalent to cash that should have come in but did not.
after:
Concept: In the indirect method of cash flow from operations, changes in working capital accounts are reconciled against net profit. An increase in trade receivables represents revenue recognized in the profit and loss statement but cash not yet collected from customers.

Step-by-step: When trade receivables rise by Rs 200cr, it means the company has extended credit to customers (or customers have delayed payment). This amount is already included in revenue and therefore in net profit after tax (PAT). However, no actual cash has entered the business yet. To convert accrual-based PAT to actual cash generated from operations, we must subtract this increase from CFO.

Result: Trade receivables increase of Rs 200cr is recorded as a cash outflow (or reduction in cash inflow) of Rs 200cr in the cash flow statement.

Why this is correct: Trade receivables are a use of cash—the company has given goods/services on credit and is awaiting payment. This non-cash revenue component must be deducted from net profit to arrive at true operating cash flow. The option correctly identifies this as a cash outflow adjustment.

Why the others are wrong: A) Cash inflow of Rs 200cr reverses the direction—an increase in receivables is the opposite of cash collection, so this is backwards. C) No impact on CFO ignores the critical reconciliation of accrual earnings to cash; working capital changes always affect CFO. D) A financing activity misclassifies the item—changes in trade receivables (an operating asset) belong in operating activities, not financing.

Intuition: Analysts must distinguish between accrual earnings and cash reality. A growing receivables balance often signals strong sales, but it also signals cash tied up in the business. A material increase in receivables can mask deteriorating cash generation despite reported profit growth—a red flag in equity research.
